Irregular correspondence from the distillery: sourcing expeditions, distillation notes, seasonal observations, and occasional essays on what it means to bottle a landscape.

March 2026

Field Notes

Field Notes: The Peat Bogs of Caithness

We rose before dawn and walked three miles into the Flow Country with nothing but a headlamp and rubber boots. The bog at this hour is not quiet — it breathes, softly, releasing something ancient and green and faintly sweet into the cold air. Alasdair calls it "the exhale." I have never found a better word for it.

"The bog at this hour is not quiet — it breathes, softly, releasing something ancient and green."

We were there for sphagnum, obviously — that extraordinary moss that dominates the bog surface, that holds water the way no other plant can, that smells, when wet, of everything that has decomposed beneath it for eight thousand years. But we also found something unexpected: a mat of crowberry growing along a slightly raised section of ground, its tiny black fruits still on the stems from last autumn. I have not smelled crowberry since we first moved here.

The quality of botanical materials varies dramatically with the season of harvest and the specific conditions of the day. Last year's sphagnum harvest — taken in October after a dry summer — produced an extract that was notably more resinous, darker, with a faint edge of smoke. This year's material, cut in early March after two months of rain, is greener, more mineral, almost mossy-aquatic. Neither is wrong. They are different notes in the same instrument.

We spent four hours harvesting, working in silence for the most part, which is how both of us prefer it. The drive back to the distillery in the grey morning light, the van smelling of wet moss and cold rubber boots, is something I hope I never take for granted.

— M.G.

January 2026

Distillery Notes

On the Habit of Silence: Distilling at Dawn

The copper still takes forty minutes to warm. In that time, Alasdair reads, and I watch the first light come over the hill. There is a quality to this particular stillness — the still ticking as it heats, the faint smell of botanicals beginning to release — that no synthetic accord has ever captured, because it is not only a smell. It is a time of day.

We distil early by preference, not necessity. The morning runs seem to us cleaner, more precise, though I cannot offer a scientific explanation for this. The air is colder. We are more awake. Perhaps the spirit that comes off the still in the first hour of daylight simply holds more attention. We have distilled Ambarvalia eleven times, and the batches that we consider the finest were all made between 5:30 and 9:00 a.m.

"The spirit that comes off the still in the first hour of daylight holds more attention."

Distillation is a patience practice. You cannot speed it up without losing something. The first distillate off the still — the foreshots — goes into a jar for Alasdair's workshop, where he uses it to clean things. The heart of the run, the fraction we bottle, emerges somewhere between hour six and hour nine, depending on the material. You learn to know it by smell.

Someone asked us recently whether we felt the size of the enterprise was a choice or a constraint. It is, entirely, a choice. At three hundred bottles per fragrance per year, we are about as large as we want to be. Perhaps a little too large. We have thought about going smaller.

— M.G.

October 2025

Essay

Correspondences: What Wild Things Smell Like

The smell of a pine forest is not, as it is often described, simply "pine." It is resin and bark and the fungal mat beneath the needles and the specific moisture of the air filtered through forty feet of canopy and the particular decay of whatever died last winter at the base of that tree. It is a chord, not a note.

This is the central problem and the central pleasure of botanical perfumery. You cannot bottle a forest. You can only — if you are careful, if you are patient, if you are lucky with your harvest — bottle one harmonic of it, and trust that the person wearing it has some memory of a forest to which it might correspond.

"You cannot bottle a forest. You can only bottle one harmonic of it."

I think often about the philosopher Alain Corbin's observation that smell is the sense most deeply implicated in involuntary memory. Not because it connects to memory in some general way, but because olfactory information bypasses the thalamus entirely and routes directly to the limbic system — the seat of emotion and memory — before the cortex has had a chance to process it. You smell the thing before you know what you are smelling. The response comes before the thought.

This is what we are working with. Not aesthetics, exactly. Not luxury, precisely. Something closer to correspondence — in the old alchemical sense, the idea that things in the world echo one another across different registers of experience. The smell of peat corresponds to something. We are trying to find out what.

— M.G.

July 2025

Distillery Notes

The New Batch: Notes on Loch Asymptote

Loch Asymptote has always been our most difficult fragrance to distil consistently. The highland pine we source — Scots pine, Pinus sylvestris, from the remnant Caledonian forest on the slopes above Loch More — varies enormously in its resin content depending on the age of the tree, the time of year, and factors we have not yet identified. The same stand of trees, harvested in June and again in September, produces material that smells recognisably similar but creates a different experience entirely in the still.

This year's batch was started in the second week of July. Alasdair ran the still very slowly — the first distillate appeared at just over six hours, which is unusually late. The resulting material was heavier than usual, with more resin and a faint note of something we have been calling "green chalk" among ourselves: a particular quality of the pine that appears, seemingly, only in certain conditions.

It will need a long maturation — perhaps eighteen months. We will not bottle it before winter 2026. This is not a problem. We have learned that the fragrances tell you when they are ready.

— A.F.

The Quarterly
Letter

Alasdair's newsletter goes out four times a year — at the solstices and equinoxes — and contains distillation notes, field dispatches, batch availability, and occasional opinions on unrelated subjects. It has twelve thousand subscribers. He remains surprised by this.
